title: Forms and How They Submit
summary: Build forms that work before any script runs, and follow what the browser sends to the server when someone presses Submit.
intro: Forms are how people send things to a website: a search, a login, a sign-up, an order. They're also where a lot goes wrong: a field the server never receives, a form that sends nothing, an order placed twice because someone pressed reload, a field nobody can fill in with a keyboard. Plain HTML gets almost all of this right by itself, in every browser, before a line of JavaScript has loaded. This lesson builds an order form for the bakery: the fields and their labels, exactly what the browser sends when you press the button, the checks it runs first, how to make a form easy for everyone, and what the server should do with what arrives.

steps.title: The form and its fields
steps.body:
A form is a set of fields inside a `<form>` element, plus a button that sends them. Each kind of field suits a different kind of answer, and picking the right one gets you the right keyboard on a phone, a date picker, or a check before anything is sent, all for free.

## A first form

Here's the smallest useful form, a search box:

```html
<form action="results.html">
  <label for="q">Search for</label>
  <input id="q" name="q" type="search">
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
```

`<form>` holds everything that's sent together. `<input>` is a field to type in. `<label>` is the field's name, the words people read next to it. And `<button>` sends the form. Type rye and press Search, or just press Enter in the field, and the browser goes to `results.html?q=rye`. The next part explains exactly how.

## Kinds of input

`<input>` is a void element, and its `type` attribute decides what kind of field it is. Each type gets its own keyboard, picker, or check:

| type | What it's for | What the browser adds |
|---|---|---|
| `text` | a short answer, and the default | nothing extra |
| `search` | a search box | a button to clear it |
| `email` | an email address | a keyboard with @ on phones, and a check for the @ |
| `tel` | a phone number | a number pad on phones |
| `url` | a web address | a check that it's a full address |
| `password` | a password | dots in place of the letters |
| `number` | a quantity | arrows to go up and down |
| `date` | a date | a calendar to pick from |
| `checkbox` | a yes or a no | a box to tick |
| `radio` | one choice from a few | a round button |
| `file` | a file from your computer | a button that opens your files |
| `hidden` | a value people don't see | nothing on screen at all |

## Longer text and lists of choices

`<textarea>` is a field for several lines of text, like a note with an order. Its `rows` attribute sets how many lines tall it starts, and unlike `<input>` it has an end tag, with any starting text between the tags.

`<select>` is a list to choose from, and each choice is an `<option>`. Each option has two parts: the words people see, between the tags, and its `value`, what gets sent. `<option value="rye">Dark rye</option>` shows Dark rye and sends `rye`.

## Checkboxes and radio buttons

A **checkbox** is on or off by itself, like Slice it for me. **Radio buttons** come in a group where only one can be chosen, like the buttons on an old radio: press one and the others pop out. Radio buttons with the same `name` form a group, and the boolean `checked` attribute picks one to start with.

## name and value: what gets sent

This is the rule that matters most: **a field is sent only if it has a `name`**. The browser sends each field as its name and its value: the text typed into a text field, the chosen option's `value` for a list, and the `value` attribute of a ticked checkbox or the chosen radio button. A checkbox that isn't ticked isn't sent at all, and neither is a field with the boolean `disabled`.

The `value` attribute on a text field sets the text it starts with. `placeholder` is something else: grey hint text that disappears as soon as you type. It isn't sent, and it isn't a label either, since it's gone by the time someone wants to check what the field was for.

## Labels

Every field needs a label, and there are two ways to connect one:

- Give the field an `id`, and the label a `for` with the same value: `<label for="email">Email</label>` and `<input id="email">`.
- Or put the field inside the label: `<label><input type="checkbox" name="sliced"> Slice it for me</label>`.

Either way, clicking the label puts the cursor in the field, or ticks the box, which gives people a much bigger target than a tiny checkbox. And a screen reader reads the label out when someone moves into the field. A field with no label is announced only as a text field, with nothing to say what it's for.

## Buttons

A `<button>` inside a form sends it, because a button's `type` is `submit` unless you say otherwise. There are two other types:

- `type="reset"` puts every field back as it started. People press it by mistake, so it's rarely worth having.
- `type="button"` does nothing at all by itself. It's for buttons that a script makes do something.

That default catches people out: a button meant for a script, like Show more, that's inside a form sends the form when pressed, unless it says `type="button"`.

examples.title: The order form
examples.prompt: Save this in your `bakery` folder as `order.html`, start Python's server there, and open `http://localhost:8000/order.html`. Click each label, try the date field, and press Tab to move from field to field.
examples.code: Order for pickup
examples.explanation: Every field has a `name`, so every one will be sent, and a label, so clicking its words works and a screen reader can name it. Clicking Your name puts the cursor in its field, and clicking Slice it for me ticks the box. The date field opens a calendar, and the quantity has arrows. The two radio buttons share the name `time`, so choosing Afternoon unticks Morning. Tab moves through the fields in the order they appear in the HTML. The form is sent with `method="post"` to `/order`, and the next part shows what that means, and why Python's server will refuse it.

steps.title: What a submit sends
steps.body:
When you press Submit, the browser builds an HTTP request out of the form, sends it, and shows whatever comes back as a new page. Knowing exactly what goes into that request is how you find out why a server says a field is missing, and how you choose between the two ways to send a form.

## action and method

Two attributes on `<form>` decide where the request goes and how:

- `action` is the address to send it to. It works like any `href`, so it can be relative, root-relative, or absolute. Leave it out, and the form is sent to the page's own address.
- `method` is the HTTP method: `get`, the default, or `post`. These are the GET and POST from the lesson on how the browser reaches a server.

## The fields become one string

Whichever method you choose, the browser starts the same way. It takes each field that has a name, in the order they appear, and writes it as the name, an `=`, and the value. Then it joins them all with `&`. Spaces become `+`, and characters with a job in a URL, like `@` and `&`, are percent-encoded, just as in a query string. For the order form that gives:

```text
name=Sam+Lee&email=sam%40example.com&loaf=rye&quantity=2&day=2026-11-28&time=afternoon&sliced=yes&notes=Ring+the+bell+%26+wait
```

This way of writing fields is called **URL encoding**, and its media type is `application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.

## GET puts the fields in the address

With `method="get"`, the browser puts that string after a `?` on the end of the `action` address, and goes there, just like following a link. Search for rye bread with the form from the previous part, and it sends `GET /results.html?q=rye+bread`.

That has real advantages: the answer has an address of its own, so people can bookmark it, share it, and come back to it. But everything in it also lands in the browser's history, in the server's logs, and in the address bar for anyone to see over your shoulder. So a password or anything private never goes in a GET.

## POST puts them in the body

With `method="post"`, nothing is added to the `action` address. The string goes in the request's **body** instead, after the headers:

```http
POST /order HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8000
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Content-Length: 126
Origin: http://localhost:8000

name=Sam+Lee&email=sam%40example.com&loaf=rye&quantity=2&day=2026-11-28&time=afternoon&sliced=yes&notes=Ring+the+bell+%26+wait
```

`Content-Type` tells the server how the body is written, and `Content-Length` how many bytes it has. `Origin` names the site the form was on, which servers use to turn away forms sent from other sites. Browsers send more headers than these. They're trimmed here to the ones that matter.

```diagram html-forms-get-post
The same fields, sent two ways: in the address with GET, or in the body with POST.
```

## Files need a different format

A file can't be squeezed into a URL-encoded string. A form that uploads one needs `method="post"` and `enctype="multipart/form-data"`. The **enctype** attribute sets the body's format, and **multipart** splits the body into parts, one for each field, each with its own small headers. A line called the **boundary**, which the browser makes up so that it can't appear in any field, separates them:

```http
POST /cakes HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:8000
Content-Type: multipart/form-data; boundary=----WebKitFormBoundaryJJIDunQA4YEBsyrE

------WebKitFormBoundaryJJIDunQA4YEBsyrE
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="name"

Sam Lee
------WebKitFormBoundaryJJIDunQA4YEBsyrE
Content-Disposition: form-data; name="photo"; filename="cake.jpg"
Content-Type: image/jpeg

(the file's bytes)
------WebKitFormBoundaryJJIDunQA4YEBsyrE--
```

Leave out the `enctype`, and the server gets only the file's name, not the file.

## Then the browser moves on

A submit is a **navigation**, just like clicking a link: the browser loads whatever the server answers as a new page, and the address bar shows where the form was sent. So if the server answers with an error page, that's the page you get. JavaScript can take over a submit and send it without leaving the page, which the JavaScript lessons show, but a plain form always navigates.

To see what a form really sent, open the Network panel in DevTools before you submit. Click the request, then the **Payload** tab: it lists each field by name, and **view source** shows the exact string.

examples.title: A search and an order arrive
examples.prompt: Save the search form from the previous part as `search.html`, and a page called `results.html` with any heading. In `bakery`, start the server. Search for rye bread, then open `order.html`, fill it in, and press Place order.
examples.explanation: The search sent a GET, so its field arrived in the address: `/results.html?q=rye+bread`. Python's server only sends files, so it ignored the query string and sent `results.html`, but a real search page would read `q` from it and find the matching loaves. The order sent a POST to `/order`, and Python's server can't take a POST at all, so it answered `501`, which means Not Implemented, and the browser showed its Error response page. That's the navigation that follows a submit: whatever comes back becomes the page. The fields still went out: the Payload tab for that request shows all eight of them. Your browser may also ask for `/favicon.ico`.

steps.title: Built-in validation
steps.body:
People make typing mistakes, and a form that catches them before anything is sent saves everyone a trip to the server and back. HTML can check most of what forms need with a few attributes, and the browser shows the messages for you, in the visitor's own language.

## Rules in attributes

Each of these adds a rule to a field:

- `required`: the field can't be left empty. For radio buttons, one of the group has to be chosen.
- `minlength` and `maxlength`: the fewest and most characters allowed in a text field. `maxlength` simply stops you typing more.
- `min` and `max`: the lowest and highest allowed for a `number` or a `date`. A date is written year, month, day, like `2026-11-28`.
- `step`: the size of each step for a number. `step="1"` is the default and allows whole numbers only. `step="0.5"` allows halves, and `step="any"` allows anything.
- `pattern`: a description of what the text must look like, written as a **regular expression**, a short code for patterns of characters. `[0-9]{5}` means exactly five digits, from 0 to 9. Put a description of the pattern in the field's `title` attribute too, since browsers show it in their message.
- `type="email"` and `type="url"` check that the text looks like an email address or a full web address.

## When the browser checks

The browser checks every rule when the form is about to be sent. If a field breaks one, it doesn't send anything: it moves to the first field with a problem, and shows a message next to it. These are the messages Chrome shows, and other browsers say much the same:

| Problem | Chrome's message |
|---|---|
| `required`, left empty | Please fill out this field. |
| `type="email"`, typed sam | Please include an '@' in the email address. 'sam' is missing an '@'. |
| `min="1"`, typed 0 | Value must be greater than or equal to 1. |
| `minlength="2"`, typed S | Please lengthen this text to 2 characters or more (you are currently using 1 character). |
| `pattern`, didn't match | Please match the requested format. |
| `step="0.5"`, typed 1.3 | Please enter a valid value. The two nearest valid values are 1 and 1.5. |

Fix the field and submit again, and the browser moves on to the next problem, until there are none and the request goes out.

## Styling fields with a problem

CSS can pick out fields that break a rule, with `:user-invalid`. It matches a field only after the person has changed it and moved on, or tried to submit, so a form doesn't start out covered in red before anyone has typed a thing:

```css
input:user-invalid {
  border: 2px solid crimson;
}
```

There's an older `:invalid` too, which matches from the moment the page loads, so every empty required field is red straight away. That's why `:user-invalid` is the one to use. The CSS lessons explain selectors like these.

## Turning the checks off

The boolean `novalidate` attribute on `<form>` turns the browser's checks off for that form. You'd use it when a script runs its own checks and shows its own messages, which the JavaScript lessons cover. The rules stay useful even then, since scripts can read them.

## The server must check again

Everything in this part runs in the visitor's browser, and the visitor controls their browser. Anyone can remove `required` in DevTools, or skip the form entirely and send any request they like with curl, as you did in the earlier lessons. Old browsers and bots ignore the rules too.

So the browser's checks are a kindness to people, never a protection. The server has to check every field again, as if the browser had checked nothing: that the quantity really is between 1 and 12, that the date isn't in the past, that the email has an @. Only the server's checks keep bad information out. The last part of this lesson shows what the server does when one fails.

examples.title: The order form, with rules
examples.prompt: Add these rules to the matching fields in `order.html`, then press Place order with the form empty. Fix each field the browser points at, and submit again each time.
examples.code:
<input id="name" name="name" type="text" required minlength="2">

<input id="email" name="email" type="email" required>

<input id="quantity" name="quantity" type="number" value="1"
       required min="1" max="12">

<input id="day" name="day" type="date" required min="2026-11-22">
examples.explanation: With the form empty, the browser stops at Your name and says Please fill out this field. Type one letter and it asks for 2 characters or more. Then it moves to the email, then the day. The quantity starts at 1, so it passes until you change it to 0 or 13. The `min` on the date stops anyone picking a day in the past, and Chrome's message gives the earliest date allowed, written the way your computer writes dates. In a real page, a server would write today's date into that `min` each time it sends the page. The request leaves only once every field passes, and the server's terminal shows nothing until then.

steps.title: Accessible, friendly forms
steps.body:
A form that works for everyone gets more orders and fewer mistakes. A few attributes group fields that belong together, let browsers fill in what they already know, bring up the right keyboard, and make sure every hint and error is read out to the person who needs it. ## Grouping fields `
` groups related fields, and its first child, ``, names the group. It's made for radio buttons and checkboxes, where each label alone doesn't say enough: ```html
Pickup time
``` A screen reader announces the legend as someone enters the group, something like Pickup time, group, then Morning, radio button, checked. Without it, they'd hear only Morning, and have to guess the question. Browsers draw a border around a fieldset, which CSS can change. ## Filling in what the browser knows Browsers remember people's names, email addresses, phone numbers, and addresses, and can fill them in with one tap. The `autocomplete` attribute tells the browser what each field is for, using a set of standard words: - `name`, `email`, and `tel` for a person's name, email address, and phone number. - `street-address`, `postal-code`, and `country-name` for an address. - `cc-number` and `cc-exp` for a card's number and expiry date. - `current-password` on a login form, and `new-password` on a sign-up form, so the password manager knows whether to fill one in or suggest a new one. - `one-time-code` for a code sent by text message, which phones can fill in straight from the message. It saves typing for everyone, and saves a lot of effort for people who find typing slow or painful. ## The right keyboard `inputmode` picks which on-screen keyboard a phone shows, without changing what the field accepts. `inputmode="numeric"` shows a number pad, `decimal` adds a decimal point, and `tel`, `email`, and `url` show keyboards for those. Use it for things made of digits that aren't amounts, like a card's security code or a one-time code. `type="number"` is the wrong choice for those: it's made for quantities, so it adds up and down arrows, and it can drop a leading zero. So a code like 0451 belongs in ``. ## Hints and errors that get read out A hint under a field, like Pick a day from tomorrow on, is useless if a screen reader never reaches it. `aria-describedby` connects the field to it: give the hint an `id`, and put that id in the field's `aria-describedby`. The screen reader then reads the label, then the hint, as the field gets focus. When the server sends the form back with an error, show the error next to its field, connect it the same way, and add `aria-invalid="true"` to the field, which tells screen readers that its value has a problem. ```html

We bake for pickup from tomorrow on.

Pick a day after today. We're closed on Mondays.

``` Write errors that say what's wrong and how to fix it: Pick a day after today, not Invalid input. And don't show a problem with color alone, since many people can't tell red from green. Words, and perhaps an icon, make sure everyone sees it. ## Visible focus The field or button the keyboard is on has **focus**, and browsers draw an outline around it, called the **focus ring**. People who use a keyboard instead of a mouse rely on it to see where they are. So never remove it without drawing something just as clear in its place. The CSS lessons show how. The Tab key moves focus through the fields in the order they come in the HTML, so keep that order the same as the order on screen. Then test every form you build with the keyboard alone: Tab to each field, type, choose options with the arrow keys, tick boxes with the space bar, and submit with Enter. If you can't finish the form that way, some of your visitors can't either.

examples.title: An accessible contact section
examples.prompt: The contact part of the order form, rebuilt with a fieldset, autocomplete words, and a hint. Replace the name and email fields in `order.html` with it, and try it on a phone if you have one nearby.
examples.code:
Your details

We'll only use it to say your order is ready.
examples.explanation: A screen reader now announces Your details, group, before the first field, then Your name, with a note that it's required. The email field reads its hint after its label, so people hear why the bakery wants it. Clicking into the name field makes the browser offer the name it has saved, and the email and phone fields offer theirs, since `autocomplete` says what each one is. On a phone, the email field brings up a keyboard with an @ key, and the phone field a number pad. The phone field has no `required`, so it's optional, and its label says what it's for.

steps.title: After the submit: the server's side
steps.body:
The form's job ends when the request leaves. What happens next is up to the server, and a few habits there decide whether pressing reload orders a second loaf, and whether someone who made a mistake has to type everything again. You'll write this code in a backend course, but the frontend has to fit with it, so here's what a good server does.

## The server reads fields by name

The server takes the body of a POST, or the query string of a GET, and splits it back into names and values, undoing the percent-encoding. Then it looks each field up by its `name`: `name` is Sam Lee, `loaf` is rye, `quantity` is 2.

That's why the `name` attributes in your HTML have to match exactly what the server's code expects. A field named `qty` when the server looks for `quantity` simply isn't there for it, and it can't tell a typo in the HTML from someone who left the field out. Remember too that an unticked checkbox isn't sent at all, so the server has to treat missing as no.

## Post, then redirect, then get

When an order is saved, the server could answer the POST with a thank-you page straight away. But then the thank-you page is the answer to a POST, and pressing reload sends that POST again. As the lesson on how the browser reaches a server showed, a POST isn't idempotent: sending it twice can order two loaves. That's why browsers ask Confirm Form Resubmission when you reload a page like that.

The fix is a pattern called **Post/Redirect/Get**:

1. The browser sends the POST with the order.
2. The server saves the order, then answers `303 See Other`, with a `Location` header naming a page for this order.
3. The browser follows it with a GET, and shows that page.

```diagram html-forms-prg
Reload repeats the last request, and after a redirect, that's the safe GET.
```

Now the page on screen came from a GET, so reloading it only asks for the order page again. `303` is the redirect made for this: it tells the browser to use GET for the next request, whatever the first one was. Every well-built form that changes something works this way.

## When something's wrong

When a field fails the server's checks, the server sends the form back, with three things a good one never forgets:

- **A status code that says so.** `422 Unprocessable Content` means the server understood the request, but the values don't pass its rules. `400 Bad Request` is for a request it couldn't make sense of at all. The browser shows the page either way, but the code tells tools and scripts it didn't work.
- **The values the person typed**, put back into each field with `value` attributes, so they fix one field instead of starting over.
- **A message next to each field with a problem**, connected with `aria-describedby` and marked with `aria-invalid`, as the previous part showed.

## GET for finding, POST for changing

The rule for choosing the method comes from HTTP itself: GET is safe, so it should never change anything.

- **Use GET** for forms that look things up: a search, a filter, the page of results. The answer gets an address people can bookmark and share, and reloading it is harmless.
- **Use POST** for forms that change something: an order, a sign-up, a login, a delete button, a comment. And for anything private, so it stays out of the address.

## When JavaScript takes over

On many sites, JavaScript catches the submit, sends the fields itself, and updates the page without a navigation. The JavaScript lessons show how. Build the plain form first anyway, with a real `action` and `method`. Then it still works when the script fails to load, which happens more often than you'd think, and the script only makes it smoother. Building it in that order is called **progressive enhancement**.

That's HTML. The next lesson starts on CSS, which decides how all of it looks.

examples.title: Post, redirect, get, as HTTP
examples.prompt: The three messages of a successful order, written out as HTTP. The first request is trimmed to its key headers, as in the part on what a submit sends.
examples.code:
POST /order HTTP/1.1 Host: bakery.example.com Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded name=Sam+Lee&email=sam%40example.com&loaf=rye&quantity=2 HTTP/1.1 303 See Other Location: /orders/1042 GET /orders/1042 HTTP/1.1 Host: bakery.example.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Content-Type: text/html; charset=utf-8

Thanks, Sam. Your order is in.
examples.explanation: The POST carries the order in its body. The server saves it as order 1042, and instead of a page, it answers `303 See Other` with a `Location` header and no body. The browser follows the `Location` by itself, with a GET, as it does for every redirect, and the address bar ends up at `/orders/1042`. That GET gets the thank-you page. Press reload now, and the browser repeats only the GET, so it shows the same page again and orders nothing. The order page has an address of its own, so Sam could bookmark it to check on the order later.

recap:
- Every field needs a name to be sent, and a label, connected with for and id or by wrapping the field.
- A button in a form submits it unless it says type="button".
- GET puts the fields in the address, for searches people can bookmark and share.
- POST puts them in the body, for anything that changes something or is private, and files need multipart.
- A submit is a navigation: whatever the server answers becomes the page.
- required, min, max, pattern, and the input types make the browser check fields before sending.
- The browser's checks help people, but only the server's checks protect anything.
- After a successful POST, the server redirects with 303, so reloading the page repeats a safe GET.
